chapter: Hippolyte Charles and the country clubs
title: Hippolyte Charles's band at the country club
summary: Personnel, the country-club and Lions Club contracts, Charles's heart trouble, Charlie Love replacing him, and tea dances at union pay.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Who else was in the band when you were there?
He had, um, he had Sonny Henry on the trombone. He had Camilla Tile. She's still living on the piano.
I've never met her. I've never met her. I've never met her.
He had a tall, brown-skinned woman. She could, she could read good, a good piano player. He had, um, uh, Big R on violin.

Yeah, violin. He had, um, um, he was playing trumpet, and I was playing tenor banjo. He had, uh, Joe Welsh on a drum. He had a fella called, uh, Clarence Paul on the saxophone. Paul. Paul. That's about, I believe that's about all he had. He was playing at the New Orleans Country Club. He had, he had, uh, the Santa Cendars contract with the Santa Cendars. He had the, uh, the Lions Club, and all them clubs. He had, uh, contract with all of them. Every, any, any dance given, any ball given at them places, that was Hippolyte Charles.
Did that Lions Club the one way uptown, where they had the carnival parades?

Did they have that, no, that's a white, they had the Lions Club downtown, too. Well, is that colored down? Yeah, colored, yeah, they had colored down. That's what he played for? Yeah. I didn't know about that. Where else was that? That, uh, it was, uh, it was, uh, it was some way down on Liberty Street, uh, where the friends on me, you heard about the fronds on me, all around there. Yeah, yeah, yeah. Some way down in that part of the section. New St. Bernard circle, man. Yeah, yeah. And, uh, all them, practically all them halls, he had, he had, uh, leased it until he stopped playing. He gave up from, trumpet on account of his heart. The doctor stopped him from playing, said his heart, he had heart trouble. And, uh, we, he sent Charlie Love in his place, tried to hold the country club down. We had, they were so crazy about our band out there, but Charlie Love, it seemed like, uh, Miss, uh, the, uh, how you call this man, uh, uh, who was running that place out there, uh, uh, what's his name now? Uh, Crawford H. Ellis.
No, I never heard of him. They haven't heard the name. Oh, he's a millionaire, yeah.

He, he was the head, he's the big man in the Standard Fruit Company, the Charlie Craft. Oh, I haven't heard of him. Crawford H. Ellis. He's got a big office in the Whitney building there. He's got a daughter, and, uh, she found fault about the band, cause Charles couldn't, Charles said he'd just come out the band and threw the flap sticks, you see? Beat them flap sticks? While we play, he just, he'd keep time with them flap sticks. So she said, the band don't sound like Mr. Charles, you know? And, uh, so he'd just laugh, you know, then, when we'd go back to lunch, and they looked like Miss Ellis ain't satisfied, that she wants me to play the horn, and I can't do it. So Camilla Todd said, Mr. Charles, won't you just bring your horn and lead on your lap? They don't know no better than you. So he tried that, that wouldn't do. They watched him, you know? He had a beautiful tone he could put in that trumpet.
Yeah, I never heard him. Why couldn't he, uh, couldn't he play for his heart?

No, he couldn't. After the doctor told him he had heart trouble, he had to put that trumpet down, that was all. He couldn't go to the top? No, he said he wasn't gonna take no chance. But they got a lot of fellas that got heart trouble and still playing. But not him, he wasn't gonna take no chance. And he's still living ever since he put that horn down. He just put a ribbon around him, put it on top of his piano, and he said, that's all. He said, he wasn't gonna blow it no more, and he didn't either. So the band just went to pieces of it. But they had Albert Glenny, who was playing bass. I was playing tenor banjo, and Albert Glenny was playing bass. You know, you heard Albert Glenny. We knew him. Yeah. And, uh, Sonny Henry trombone.
Yeah. But when was that, Eddie? Do you remember about what period that was?

After the First World War? Oh, yeah, well... Before the Depression? No, it was before that, yeah. That was around, just about around in the war time, I think, if I'm mistaken, because we was playing. We was, uh, that was the only place practically running, you know, regular out there in all these country clubs. They never did stop, you know, with a war or nothing. But they used to have, we used to play the tea dance on Sunday afternoon, you know, in the evening. Six, uh, six to eight, uh, ten, I think. And, uh, we, uh, we was getting, uh, a union price when, uh, when they was playing, the bands was playing for a dollar and a half. We was getting two dollars an hour out there. Yeah, I did. So we always got union price out there. Country club paid good. Charles got, got good money for your band.
